ACORN: After the decisive Battle of Vimy Ridge during the First World War, Canadian soldier, Lieutenant Leslie Miller, gathered acorns from oak trees amongst the rubble and wreckage. Miller brought the acorns back home to Scarborough, Ontario and planted the trees as a legacy to those who perished. The acorns from those trees were then repatriated and planted back in France in 2018. Lieutenant Leslie Miller's Vimy Oaks are now growing on Vimy Ridge, and today approximately 1,000 descendant Vimy Oaks have been planted across Canada as commemorative trees. Check out the [Vimy Oaks Legacy](https://vimyoakslegacy.ca/) website to learn more!
ACRES: Canada’s vast landscape covers over 2 billion acres, with millions dedicated to fertile farmland. While Canada officially uses the metric system, the acre remains a popular way to measure land, especially in farming and real estate. These acres grow much of the food enjoyed across the country and around the world – from wheat and canola to fruits and vegetables. Canada’s farmland is a vital part of the nation’s economy, culture, and connection to the land.
ACTOR: Canada is home to some incredible actors! Some of our all-time favourites include: Mike Myers, Rachel McAdams, Jim Carrey, Seth Rogen, Ryan Reynolds, Graham Greene, Ryan Gosling, Cobie Smulders, John Candy, Elliot Page, Keanu Reeves, Simu Liu, Neve Campbell, Sarah Polley, Hayden Christensen, Donald & Kiefer Sutherland, Michael J. Fox, Tom Green, Evangeline Lilly, Jay Baruchel, Michael Cera, William Shatner, Brendan Fraser, Nathan Fillion, Catherine O'Hara, Eugene & Dan Levy, Leslie Nielsen, Martin Short, Gordon Pinsent, Megan Follows, Christopher Plummer, Lorne Greene, Adam Beach, Dan Aykroyd, Sandra Oh, and Matthew Perry just to name a few! April 19th is the 10th annual [National Canadian Film Day](https://canfilmday.ca/)! You're invited to an All You Can Watch Buffet of Canadian film, featuring Canadian actors, directors, producers, and more. Head over to [canfilmday.ca](https://canfilmday.ca/) to check out all the films! #CanFilmDay
AFTER: Did you know that 1 in 3 of those visiting food banks are children? Food Banks Canada's [After The Bell](https://foodbankscanada.ca/after-the-bell/) program provides nutritious, child-friendly food packs throughout the summer when school-centered supports are not available so kids can soar on the swings and splash in the community pool with their friends. Participating food banks receive packs that contain shelf-stable items such as milk, hummus, crackers, cereal, oatmeal and sunflower seeds and they also receive grant money to supplement the food packs. The goal in 2024 is for the program to deliver 200,000 packs in 215 communities across Canada.
AGENT: [Camp X](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/camp-x) - a popular name that reflects the secrecy surrounding its activities - was a training school for covert agents and a radio communications centre that operated on the shores of Lake Ontario between Whitby and Oshawa during the Second World War. It was the first such purpose-built facility constructed in North America.
AHEAD: "Ahead by a Century" is a song by Canadian rock band [The Tragically Hip](https://thehip.com/). It was released as the lead single from the band's fifth studio album, Trouble at the Henhouse. The song reached #1 on Canada's singles chart, and is the band's most successful single in their native Canada. The song was certified platinum in Canada in 2016, and it was the last song performed by the band at their final concert on August 20, 2016.
ALDER: Alder trees are commonly found across Canada, from British Columbia to Newfoundland and Labrador. These hardy trees are known for their ability to thrive in wet environments and play a crucial role in enriching the soil by fixing nitrogen. Indigenous peoples in Canada have long used alder wood for building, and its bark for medicinal purposes. Whether you're exploring the forests of the West Coast or the shores of the Atlantic, alder trees are a natural part of Canada’s diverse ecosystems.
ALLEY: Each spring along the eastern coast of Newfoundland and Labrador, it's prime time for spotting icebergs. With many little towns along a thousand kilometres of coastline, this area known as "Iceberg Alley" is an outstanding location for viewing roving blue natural ice sculptures that float down from Greenland and Canada's Arctic. The massive chunks of broken glaciers are only 10% visible since most of the iceberg is submerged and floating on its side.
ANIME: Did you know that [Anime North](https://www.animenorth.com/) is Canada's largest fan-run anime convention? Founded in 1997 by Toronto anime enthusiast Donald Simmons, it began as a one-day event with around 600 attendees. Today, it attracts tens of thousands of fans annually to celebrate anime, manga, music, games, and Japanese culture. This year's convention takes place from May 23-25, 2025, at the Toronto Congress Centre.
ANTHEM: Canada’s national anthem, O Canada, was first performed in 1880 in Québec City and has since become a defining part of our shared identity. Originally written in French, an English version followed in 1906, with its lyrics continuing to evolve for more than a century. In 1980, Canada’s National Anthem Act received royal assent and officially took effect on July 1, becoming a centerpiece of that year’s Dominion Day celebrations. Whether sung in schools, at hockey games, or during national ceremonies, O Canada remains a moment that unites Canadians from coast to coast to coast.
APPLE: The McIntosh (nicknamed the “Mac”) is the national apple of Canada. John McIntosh discovered the original McIntosh sapling on his Dundela farm in Upper Canada in 1811. Many years later, Apple Inc. named the Macintosh computer line after the fruit.
ARMED: Canadian Armed Forces Day takes place on the first Sunday in June each year and is a celebration of the members of the [Canadian Armed Forces](https://forces.ca/), both those who are currently serving and those who have served in the past. To all current and past members of the Canadian Armed Forces, and to the loved ones who stand with you, we appreciate and recognize your bravery, dedication and sacrifice. Thank you for answering the call to serve, and for making Canada and the world a better place to live.
ASPEN: Aspen are a deciduous, hardwood tree of the genus Populus, belonging to the willow family. Trembling aspen and largetooth aspen are native to Canada; the former, found from the treeline to northern Mexico, is the most widely distributed tree in North America. Trembling aspen grows on most soils, doing best on well-drained, moist, sandy or gravelly loams. As a fast-growing pioneer tree species, it is ideal for quickly restoring a wide range of forest functions after disturbances.
ASTER: Happy Mother's Day from Canuckle! The aster is a vibrant, star-shaped wildflower that brightens Canadian meadows and gardens from late summer into fall. With over 20 native species in Canada, asters provide an important source of nectar for bees and butterflies, supporting pollinators across the country. Traditionally linked with love, patience, and elegance, it’s a fitting bloom to celebrate and honour mothers everywhere on Mother's Day.
ATRIA: Today is World Heart Day! September 29th is a global celebration of the heart and all of its parts, including its two atria! Did you know that the pacemaker was invented by a Canadian? John Hopps made many contributions to the field of medicine, but he is best known his cardiac pacemaker invention that keeps hundreds of thousands of hearts beating around the world.
AVENS: Happy First Day of Spring! The mountain avens became the official floral emblem of the Northwest Territories in 1957. Part of the rose family, narrow leaves support tiny white flowers that bloom from June to July. Historically significant to the Inuit, the twisting of the seed head marked when to move inland and hunt caribou. It's one of the many wildflowers that signal the arrival of spring in the Arctic.
BALER: Balers have played a significant role in Canadian history, particularly in the development of the Prairie provinces. The ability to compress and transport hay and straw efficiently helped to open up new land for agriculture and settlement. The Canadian agricultural industry relies heavily on balers, with many farmers using them to harvest and process crops like wheat, barley, oats, and alfalfa.
BALSA: Balsa wood is lightweight yet incredibly strong, making it a go-to material for Canadian crafters and hobbyists! Native to South America, balsa is used in model airplanes, ping pong paddles, and even surfboards. Many Canadian builders appreciate its ease of use and buoyancy, making it perfect for crafting floatable objects. So next time you spot a model plane or a small raft in Canada, there's a good chance balsa wood is behind the design!
BANDS: Today is [National Indigenous Veterans Day](https://www.veterans.gc.ca/en/remembrance/people-and-stories/indigenous-veterans), a time to honour the First Nations, Inuit, and Métis peoples who have served in uniform. Thousands of Indigenous veterans from communities and bands across Canada volunteered in both World Wars, Korea, and beyond – often travelling far from home to defend a country that did not yet grant them full rights. Their courage, resilience, and leadership are now formally recognized and remembered each November 8, as Canadians pay tribute to the vital role Indigenous veterans have played in our shared history.
BARON: Anyone outside of Western Canada might not know or understand the cult following behind the unassuming [Burger Baron](https://burgerbaronedmonton.com/) restaurant. The popular fast-food chain, with its distinctive sign, popular mushroom burger and 25 locations around Alberta, has been a part of the Prairie dining scene since the 1950s. Founded in 1957 in either Calgary or Lethbridge, Alberta (the location and ownership of the first site is disputed), Burger Baron was one of the first drive-in restaurant chains in Western Canada. Many of the owners are Lebanese Canadians, connected to Rudy Kemaldean of Edmonton. Among other things, Burger Baron is famous for being endorsed by former Edmonton Oilers hockey coach Glen Sather and other former members of the Edmonton Oilers.
BASIC: From fresh produce to pantry staples, [Food Basics](https://www.foodbasics.ca/) has been a familiar name in Ontario grocery aisles since 1995. The discount supermarket chain built its reputation around offering Canadians the basics they need every day at prices that help stretch the grocery budget. Today, Food Basics has more than 150 stores across Ontario.
BASTE: On Thanksgiving, many Canadians keep their turkey juicy by basting it – spooning or brushing the pan drippings back over the bird while it roasts. Turkey is at the heart of the holiday meal in Canada, with Canadians eating over 2 million whole turkeys at Thanksgiving each year! The holiday itself has been celebrated here since 1879, making it one of the country’s oldest traditions. Whether you baste, brine, or butter, it’s all about sharing a meal and giving thanks with loved ones.
BATON: Canada has a strong tradition of excellence in relay races, with its teams achieving notable success on the world stage. The Canadian men's 4x100m relay team famously won gold at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, a triumph that echoed the country's prowess in track and field. More recently, the men's 4x100m team clinched silver at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, further solidifying Canada's status as a powerhouse in relay events. These achievements highlight the strength and teamwork that define [Canadian athletics](https://olympic.ca/sports/athletics/).
BEADS: Beading has a very long artistic and cultural history among the Indigenous people in Canada. At least 8,000 years before Europeans came to Canada, First Nations people were using beads in elaborate designs and for trade. Today, you can find beautiful First Nations beadwork at powwows, First Nations arts stores and museums across Canada. June 21st is National Indigenous Peoples Day. Take the opportunity to learn more about the cultural and linguistic diversity as well as the contributions of First Nations, Inuit and Métis Peoples.
BEARS: Roughly half of the world's Grizzly Bears (a Brown Bear subspecies) live in Canada, mostly in BC.
BEETS: Sugar beets have played a key role in Canada's sugar production for over a century! While most of Canada's sugar comes from imported cane, sugar beets are grown domestically - mainly in Alberta. In the town of Taber, home to Canada's last remaining sugar beet processing plant, 200 local farm families supply the refinery with approximately 840,000 tonnes of sugar beets each year. This yields 125,000 tonnes of sugar, making up 8–10% of Canada's total sugar consumption! From root to sweet treat, these beets keep Canada's sugar industry thriving!
BELLS: It's time to ring in the New Year! Churches, cathedrals and towers across Canada will be ringing the bells tonight at midnight to signal the start of 2023. There are 11 carillons in Canada, ranging from the historic Hamilton cathedral to the more modern Exhibition Place carillon in Toronto. The Peace Tower Carillon on Parliament Hill in Ottawa is the most frequently played and the best known carillon. It has 53 bells, and was inaugurated on July 1, 1927 to mark the 60th anniversary of Confederation. The Cathedral of the Transfiguration in Markham, Ontario contains one of the world’s largest sets of bells. They were cast in bronze and weigh in at a whopping 32,000 pounds (over 14,500kg)!
BIRCH: The white birch is the most widely distributed of native birch trees, and grows in every region of Canada. The bark has long been used for making canoes and ornaments.
BITES: [History Bites](https://historybites.ca/) is a Canadian television series on the History Television network that ran from 1998 to 2004. Created by Rick Green, the sketch comedy show explored what would be on television if the medium was around for 5,000 years of human history. The show featured a large ensemble cast. It earned five Gemini nominations and won a Canadian Comedy Award.
BLAND: Despite the name, Blanding’s turtles aren’t bland at all! This bright-eyed freshwater species, found in southern Ontario, Quebec, and parts of the Maritimes, has a striking yellow throat and domed shell. Sadly, these turtles are endangered, and conservation efforts across Canada are helping protect their wetlands and nesting sites so they can continue to thrive.
BLAST: Every day, the Royal Artillery fires the noon gun at the [Halifax Citadel National Historic Site](https://parks.canada.ca/lhn-nhs/ns/halifax) in Halifax, Nova Scotia. The 19th-century British fort fires one of the oldest continuous noon guns in the world. The cannon’s blast has been part of Halifax’s daily rituals since 1857. The present noon gun is a reproduction 12 pounder, smooth-bore muzzle loading gun used during the reign of King George III (1760-1820).
BLUES: The [Maple Blues Awards](https://www.mapleblues.ca/) is Canada’s national blues awards program. Its goal is to promote blues music across Canada and to recognize outstanding achievement in the field. The Maple Blues Awards have been presented by the Toronto Blues Society since their inception in 1997.
BOARD: The folding ironing board was invented by Canadian-American engineer Elijah McCoy in 1874. A truly portable folding ironing board was first patented in Canada in 1875 by Yarmouth, Nova Scotia's John B. Porter. The invention also included a removable press board used for sleeves.
BONES: Known as the "Dinosaur Capital of the World", the town of Drumheller, Ablerta has some of the richest deposits of fossils and dinosaur bones in the world! In Alberta's Red Deer River valley, home to Dinosaur Provincial Park, more than 1,000 complete skeletons of extinct dinosaurs have been found since the late 1800s.
BOOST: Launched in Sherwood Park, Alberta in 1999, [Booster Juice](https://boosterjuice.com/) has grown from a single Prairie shop into a nationwide Canadian success story. Its smoothies, boosters, and fresh juices offer a quick pick-me-up for Canadians on the go. It’s a true homegrown brand delivering a refreshing boost across the country.
BRACE: The modern lingual brace has Canadian roots. Saskatchewan-born orthodontist Dr. Craven Kurz earned his dental degree from McGill University in 1968 before moving to California, where he pioneered braces that attach to the back of the teeth. Developed in the 1970s for patients who wanted a less visible treatment, his innovation helped make “invisible” orthodontics a reality.
BRACT: It's the first day of spring! Some Canadian alpine plants show off colourful bracts – specialized leaves that look like petals and help attract pollinators. Bunchberry and mountain avens, found in northern and high-elevation regions, use bracts to brighten the tundra and forest floor, announcing the season’s first blooms.
BRAND: Canada is home to many iconic brands and locally owned companies that reflect the country’s creativity, innovation, and regional pride. From everyday essentials to globally recognized names like Tim Hortons, Lululemon, Canada Goose, Aritzia, and Roots, Canadian brands span food, fashion, retail, and outdoor gear. Together, they are a strong part of the national identity, showcasing homegrown quality and entrepreneurial spirit and connecting communities in every part of the country.
BREAD: Bannock or fry bread is a form of bread that served as a staple in the diets of early settlers in Canada. It's believed Scottish fur traders introduced it, but many Indigenous communities had pre-colonial versions of bannock: Inuit call it "palauga", Mi’kmaq "luskinikn", and Ojibwe "ba‘wezhiganag". A delicious bread that has been made and enjoyed in Canada for hundreds of years, bannock is now frequently found at gatherings and festivals. Read more about bannock on [The Canadian Encyclopedia](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/bannock).
BRIDE: War Bride was the name given to the estimated 48,000 young women who met and married Canadian servicemen and came to Canada during the Second World War. These war brides were mostly from Britain, but a few thousand were also from other areas of Europe. Read more about "war brides" on [The Canadian Encyclopedia](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/war-brides).
BRINE: Brine isn’t just salty water – it’s the starting point for one of Canada’s biggest salt success stories. At its Goderich operation on Lake Huron, [Sifto Canada](https://siftocanada.com/) operates the world’s largest rock salt mine, producing millions of tonnes of bulk salt each year. A separate nearby facility pumps up underground brine, then evaporates and refines it into around 95,000 tonnes high-purity, food-grade salt each year. From seasoning kitchens to preserving food across the country, Canadian brine plays a quietly essential role at the table.
BROWN: Brown bears are a familiar sight in Canada’s wild landscape, with the iconic grizzly bear representing one of the country’s most recognizable animals. The grizzly is a subspecies of brown bear and can be found across western and northern regions. Their coats can range from nearly black to golden brown, proving that brown comes in many shades!
BUGGY: Mennonite groups can be found across Canada, with over half of the population residing in urban areas such as Winnipeg, Vancouver, and Kitchener-Waterloo. Almost 200,000 Mennonites call Canada home. Waterloo Region is home to the largest population of Old Order Mennonites in Canada, particularly in the areas around St. Jacobs and Elmira. They are often seen on the local roads using their traditional horse and buggy transportation, and many also use horses to pull the implements in their farm fields.
BUMPS: Did you know the Goosebumps TV series, based on R.L. Stine’s popular children’s books, was filmed in Canada? Many episodes were shot in Ontario, including locations in and around the Greater Toronto Area, which helped create the show’s eerie suburban atmosphere. Canadian settings played a key role in bringing the spooky stories to life for young viewers in the 1990s.
BUNNY: The “bunny hug” is a particularly Saskatchewan term for what people elsewhere in Canada might call a “hoodie” – a hooded sweatshirt with a big pocket on the front. Residents of Saskatchewan are proud to call their hoodies bunny hugs, even if they are the only ones in Canada that typically do so!
BUTTE: Situated in the Big Muddy Badlands in Saskatchewan, Castle Butte is a grand, reddish free-standing structure with a circumference of 0.5 km and an elevation of 60 metres. A relic from the Ice Age, it is a striking formation that served as a landmark for Indigenous people, the North West Mounted Police (NWMP) and early prairie settlers. Other notable Canadian buttes include Pilot Butte (Saskatchewan), Lone Butte (British Columbia), Nebogwawin Butte (Manitoba), Nahanni Butte (Northwest Territories), and Mud Buttes (Alberta). It goes without saying that these buttes are some of our country's finest assets! Read more about [Canada's Nicest Buttes](https://www.familyfuncanada.com/canadas-nicest-buttes/).
CACTI: Four species of cacti are native to Canada: pincushion cactus, little prickly pear cactus, common plains prickly pear cactus, and eastern prickly pear cactus. All of these species are at the northern limits of their distribution. In 1985, the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada officially designated the cactus as an endangered plant.
CADET: In the Canadian Armed Forces, the appointment of officer cadet is held by beginning officers, as well as students attending the Royal Military College of Canada in Kingston, Ontario and the Collège militaire royal de Saint-Jean in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Québec. Officer cadets and naval cadets complete the Regular Officer Training Plan to become commissioned officers in the Canadian Armed Forces.
CALVE: When glaciers calve, large chunks of ancient ice break away and crash into cold waters, shaping Canada’s Arctic and mountain landscapes. The Columbia Icefield on the Alberta–British Columbia border feeds major river systems, while northern glaciers in places like Baffin Island and Ellesmere Island calve into Arctic waters, helping form icebergs that can drift toward Atlantic waters each spring. Today, increased calving is also seen as a visible sign of a warming climate in Canada.
CAMPS: Over 5.7 million Canadian adults camp each year and the camping industry contributes a total of $4.7 billion annually to Canada's economy.
CANDY: Did you know that [Ganong](https://ganong.com/) candy company in St. Stephen, New Brunswick is Canada's oldest chocolate and candy company? Canada is also home to some unique sweet candy treats, like Smarties, Coffee Crisp, Caramilk, Aero, Crunchie, and Mackintosh's Toffee to name a few!
CANON: In literature, a canon is a collection of works considered especially important or enduring, and Canada has many that stand out. From beloved classics like Lucy Maud Montgomery's Anne of Green Gables to influential contemporary novels such as Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale, the Canadian literary canon also includes powerful works by Indigenous authors whose stories reflect the depth and diversity of this land. Together, these books remain cornerstones of Canadian storytelling.
CAPER: The "Canadian Caper" was the joint covert rescue by the Canadian government and the CIA of six American diplomats who had evaded capture during the seizure of the United States embassy in Tehran, Iran, on November 4, 1979. An article written about these events was published in Wired in 2007. The article was used loosely as the basis of the 2012 film Argo.
CAPOT: The capot (or capote) is a traditional Canadian garment that originated in the 17th century, crafted from wool blankets by French Canadian fur traders to withstand harsh winters. These long, hooded coats, often called "blanket coats", were later sold by the Hudson's Bay Company and became a staple for those braving the cold in the fur trade. The capot was also widely worn by First Nations peoples, who adapted it to suit their needs. With its warm, practical design, the capot became a lasting symbol of resilience in the Canadian wilderness!
CARAT: Happy Mother's Day from Canuckle! Canadian mines produced 18.6 million carats of rough diamonds valued at $2.25 billion in 2019, making Canada the world's third largest producer of rough diamonds by value.
CARTS: Carts were essential for travel and trade in early Canada, and the [Red River Cart](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/red-river-cart) is one of the most famous. Developed by the Métis during the settlement of the Prairies in the mid- to late-1800s, these two-wheeled wooden carts could carry up to 450 kg of goods across long distances, pulled by oxen or horses. The cart takes its name from the Red River, along which the Red River Colony was settled, and the Métis had their own Michif words for it, including aen wagon and aen charet. These carts became a lasting symbol of Métis ingenuity and resilience on the frontier.
CARVE: With its many carved pumpkins, sculptures and special effects, [Pumpkins After Dark](https://pumpkinsafterdark.com/) brings magic across Canada. Pumpkins After Dark is Canada’s award-winning outdoor Halloween event, with locations in Burnaby, Calgary, Edmonton, Milton and Ottawa. Featuring over 10,000+ hand-carved pumpkins, this one-of-a-kind walk-through experience is the must-see event of the spooky season.
CAVES: Canada is home to some spectacular natural caves waiting to be explored! While Canada may be known for its vast wilderness and towering mountains, it also boasts a hidden underground world filled with breathtaking caverns and geological wonders. Some notable examples include the Bonnechere Caves and Bruce Peninsula Caves in Ontario, the Canmore Caverns in Alberta, the Horne Lake Caves on Vancouver Island, and the Castleguard Cave in Banff National Park, the longest cave in Canada. Whether you're spelunking through narrow passageways or admiring dazzling rock formations, exploring caves in Canada is an unforgettable adventure that reveals the hidden beauty beneath the surface of the Great White North.
CEDAR: Canada has the world’s largest stock of standing western redcedar trees. The western redcedar is the arboreal emblem of the province of British Columbia.
CHANT: Today is [National Indigenous Peoples Day](https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1100100013718/1708446948967)! On June 21, we recognize and celebrate the history, heritage, resilience and diversity of First Nations, Inuit and Métis across Canada. Chants play a vital role in Indigenous culture in Canada, used in ceremonies, healing, and storytelling for generations. These rhythmic vocalizations help preserve history, connect communities, and honour ancestors. Chants, alongside traditional songs, are a way for Indigenous peoples to maintain their cultural identity and pass knowledge from one generation to the next. They are a powerful form of expression and resilience within Canada’s rich cultural mosaic.
CHARR: Arctic charr (or char) is a cold-water fish found across Canada’s North and is an important traditional food for Inuit and many northern Indigenous communities. Closely related to salmon and trout, it thrives in some of the coldest lakes and rivers on Earth, and Nunavut is home to one of the world’s largest commercial Arctic charr fisheries.
CIDER: In Canada, the history of cider could be traced back to explorers like Captain Cook and the Hudson's Bay Company. Cider was used to help prevent scurvy! It may have been the British that first brought cider to Canada, but production flourished in Quebec.
CLAIM: Today is [National Indigenous Peoples Day](https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1100100013718/1708446948967)! On June 21, we recognize and celebrate the history, heritage, resilience and diversity of First Nations, Inuit and Métis across Canada. Gertrude Guerin was a fierce protector of Indigenous people and culture. Living near Vancouver, Guerin spent her adult life helping the Indigenous Peoples of the city. From founding Indigenous organizations, to serving as chief of her First Nation, to helping launch a landmark land claims case, Gertrude had a huge impact on the Lower Mainland area and Canada. The Supreme Court decision in the Guerin case is one of the most important legal judgments in the history of Indigenous law in Canada.
CLANS: Many Indigenous communities across Canada are organized into clans, which play an important role in identity, governance, and kinship. Ribbon skirts often honour these connections, with colours and patterns reflecting clan affiliations, personal stories, or ancestral ties. On January 4th, as we celebrate National Ribbon Skirt Day, we recognize the strength and unity of Indigenous clans, which continue to inspire the designs and meanings behind these beautiful garments.
CLAST: In geology, a clast is a fragment of rock or mineral that tells a story millions of years old. Found in sedimentary rocks across Canada – from the rocky shores of Niagara Escarpment to the ancient beds of the Canadian Rockies – these fragments reveal how mountains eroded, rivers flowed, and landscapes shifted, preserving tiny pieces of Earth’s history for curious eyes today.
CLEFT: Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children has played a major role in advancing cleft lip and palate surgery. Beginning more than 50 years ago, surgeons including Drs. W. K. Lindsay and Hugh G. Thomson developed and refined techniques for repairing cleft lips at SickKids. Today, its comprehensive [Cleft Lip and Palate Program](https://www.sickkids.ca/en/care-services/clinics/cleft-palate-clinic/) continues to provide specialized care from infancy through young adulthood, while training surgeons and contributing to cleft care around the world.
COACH: Henry Ruttan was a prominent businessman, inventor, and politician in Upper Canada who revolutionized railway travel. In 1858, he patented an innovative system for heating and cooling railway coaches, which was adopted by several railway companies across North America. His system used the motion of the train to force outside air through ducts and a wash tank, where the air was cleaned, humidified, and cooled. During winter, the system was adapted to heat the air entering the cars, making train travel more comfortable year-round. Ruttan’s invention was a game-changer for passenger comfort and a brilliant example of Canadian ingenuity!
CONES: Snow-dusted evergreens are a hallmark of Canadian Christmas, and their cones play a surprisingly festive role. Pine cones are often gathered, painted, glittered, or scented with cinnamon to make ornaments, wreaths, and table centrepieces. Across Canada, these natural treasures help bring a rustic, wintry charm to Christmas décor, connecting homes to the snowy landscapes outside.
COYPU: The coypu, known in Canada as the nutria, is a large, semi-aquatic rodent originally from South America that was introduced here for the fur trade. While it might look a bit like a beaver or muskrat, it has a distinctive long, round, sparsely-haired tail. Coypu were once raised on fur farms in provinces like British Columbia, Alberta, and Ontario, making them an interesting, if little-known, part of Canada’s fur-trading history.
CRAFT: In the past decade, Canada has seen a rapidly growing number of craft breweries popping up. Craft breweries have become so popular in Canada that a new association, Canadian Craft Brewers Association, was formed in May 2019. Sales of craft beer increased tenfold from 2008 to 2018, and it now accounts for 6% of the Canadian market. December 10th is National Lager Day! Lagers are some of the most popular beer styles in the world and Canada is no exception. Celebrate with a craft lager from your favourite Canadian brewery!
CRANE: The Whooping Crane is the tallest bird in North America and the rarest crane species. They stand nearly five-feet tall and are easily recognizable with their snowy white plumage and crimson cap. The only self-sustaining wild population of whooping cranes breeds in Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park, which straddles the Northwest Territories and Alberta border.
CRASH: [Crash Adams](https://www.crashadamsmusic.com/), the Toronto-based pop duo, performed their original song “Optimist” on America’s Got Talent in 2025, earning four “yes” votes from the judges. They were previously nominated for Breakthrough Group of the Year at the 2024 Juno Awards, highlighting their rise in the Canadian music scene. Their energetic blend of pop, rock, and electronic music has won them a devoted fanbase.
CREPE: [Cora restaurants](https://www.chezcora.com/) have been a breakfast favourite in Canada since 1987, when Cora Mussely Tsouflidou transformed a small snack bar in Montreal into a breakfast haven. She crafted a menu filled with fresh fruit, omelettes, French toast, and, of course, delicious crêpes! Today, Cora serves a staggering 60,000 crêpes every week across its many locations, making it a leader in Canada’s breakfast industry. With over 10 million guests served each year, Cora continues to brighten mornings with its signature crêpe creations, like the famous April 89 Crêpe, packed with fresh fruit and custard. Whether you prefer sweet or savoury, there's always a crêpe to flip over at Cora!
CREST: With its striking crest, the hooded merganser is one of Canada’s most distinctive waterfowl. Both males and females can raise or lower their fan-shaped crests, using them for display and communication. The male’s bold black-and-white crest is especially eye-catching during breeding season, helping it stand out on lakes and wetlands across the country. Even its scientific name reflects this feature, drawing from Greek words meaning “crest” and “diver,” a perfect match for this skilled, fish-catching duck.
CRIED: [The Girl Who Cried Pearls](https://www.nfb.ca/film/the-girl-who-cried-pearls/) made history in 2026 by winning the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film. Produced by the National Film Board of Canada, the stop-motion film was created by Montréal-based directors Chris Lavis and Maciek Szczerbowski, and is set in early 20th-century Montréal. Featuring Canadian voice actor Colm Feore, it’s a powerful example of homegrown storytelling earning global recognition.
CRIER: Before newspapers or social media, Canadian towns relied on the town crier to spread the news. Ringing a bell and shouting “Hear Ye! Hear Ye!”, they announced royal proclamations, local events, and important updates. Today, town criers are a cherished part of Canada’s history, keeping this lively tradition alive at festivals and ceremonies!
CRISP: How do Canadians like their coffee? Crisp! Coffee Crisp is a chocolate bar made in Canada consisting of layers of vanilla wafer and coffee-flavoured soft candy, covered in milk chocolate. It's a unique Canadian treat, and it rarely ventures beyond Canada's borders. The candy has largely been made exclusively for Canadian markets - over 150 million Coffee Crisp bars are produced every year in the Nestlé Canada factory in Toronto.
CROPS: Canada is the world’s largest grower and exporter of flax seed, canola, oats, mustard seeds, pulses (peas, beans, and lentils) and durum wheat.
CRUDE: Canada has the 3rd largest oil reserves in the world and is the 4th largest oil producer and exporter.
CURSE: The Oak Island mystery is a series of stories and legends concerning buried treasure and unexplained objects found on or near Oak Island in Nova Scotia. Since the 18th century, attempts have been made to find treasure and artifacts. Hypotheses about artifacts present on the island range from pirate treasure to Shakespearean manuscripts to the Holy Grail or the Ark of the Covenant. A "curse" on the treasure is said to have originated more than a century ago and states that seven men will die in the search for the treasure before it is found. This intriguing tale has been the subject of the popular TV series "The Curse of Oak Island," which follows brothers Rick and Marty Lagina as they explore the island's mysteries.
DABKE: Happy [Canadian Multiculturalism Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/celebrate-canada/multiculturalism-day.html)! The dabke is a lively Lebanese folk dance that symbolizes unity and joy - and it’s found a home in Canada too! With vibrant Lebanese communities across the country, especially in cities like Montreal and Ottawa, the dabke is often performed at cultural festivals, weddings, and community celebrations. Its energetic footwork and rhythmic stomping bring people together, showcasing the rich traditions of Lebanon that have become part of Canada’s diverse cultural mosaic.
DANCE: Canada is a country rich in multicultural heritage and culture, part of which is dance. Long before we called this land Canada, Aboriginal dancers were practising dance. Powwow dances are beautiful expressions of Indigenous spirituality, history and culture. When more people began immigrating to Canada in the 1900s, they brought with them bits of rich heritage and culture from all over the globe. This influx of international talent is what led to the creation of most of our dance institutions today, including the National Ballet of Canada and the Royal Winnipeg Ballet, Canada's oldest ballet company and the longest continuously operating ballet company in North America. Sikh-Canadian Gurdeep Pandher of the Yukon, has been spreading joy, hope and positivity across Canada with his Bhangra dancing - a traditional folk dance of Punjab. Check out [www.gurdeep.ca](https://gurdeep.ca/) and get ready to dance!
DECOY: Hunters in Canada have been using decoys for generations to attract waterfowl like ducks and geese during hunting season. Decoy carving is even considered an art form, particularly in communities along the East Coast, where handmade decoys were once essential for a successful hunt. Decoys play a symbolic role in connecting Canadians with their heritage and the outdoors, a reflection of the country's strong ties to nature and conservation.
DEEDS: November 13th is [World Kindness Day](https://www.randomactsofkindness.org/world-kindness-day)! The purpose of World Kindness Day is to highlight and encourage good deeds in your community. In Canada, the Chevrolet Good Deeds Cup seeks to inspire young Canadians to do good by transforming the positive values learned through hockey into Good Deeds within their communities. The program has made an incredible impact in communities coast to coast to coast amounting more than 1,000 Good Deeds and over $600,000 to charities.
DELTA: Happy World Rivers Day! Deltas are wetlands that form as rivers empty their water and sediment into another body of water, such as an ocean, lake, or another river. Among the largest deltas in Canada are those of the Mackenzie and Saskatchewan rivers, as well as the Peace-Athabasca Delta. The Mackenzie Delta in Northwest Territories is one of the world's largest river deltas.
DEMON: In 2025, Netflix’s KPop Demon Hunters thrilled audiences with a fictional K-Pop girl group battling demons through music. Co-directed by Maggie Kang – born in Seoul, raised in Toronto, and a Sheridan College animation grad – the film blends Korean mythology with Canadian creativity. Its hit song Golden made Billboard history, topping both the Hot 100 and Global 200 charts.
DERBY: It's the final weekend of the 2023 [Calgary Stampede](https://www.calgarystampede.com/) - the world's largest outdoor rodeo! This year, the Stampede is celebrating 100 years of chuckwagon racing at the Cowboys Rangeland Derby! The world’s first Chuckwagon Race was staged at the Calgary Stampede in 1923. A true throwback to the wild west, the event was inspired by the tradition of cowboys breaking camp and racing home. And while some of the rules have since changed, the rush has never left. YAHOO!
DINER: [The Chickenburger](https://chickenburger.com/) in Bedford, Nova Scotia, has been part of Canada’s diner history since 1940 and is reputed to be the country’s oldest drive-in restaurant. Known for its chickenburgers, cheeseburgers and shakes, it preserves the look and feel of a classic 1950s diner, complete with a working jukebox. More than 86 years after opening, the landmark remains a throwback to the golden age of diner culture.
DONER: The doner kebab, a Turkish dish of spiced meat cooked on a rotating spit, inspired a Canadian classic - the Halifax donair! Adapted in Nova Scotia in the 1970s, it swaps lamb for seasoned ground beef and yogurt sauce for a sweet garlic sauce. Served on warm pita with diced onions and tomatoes, the donair quickly became a Maritime favourite and a late-night legend. The donair became so iconic it was named Halifax’s official food in 2015.
DONOR: It's [National Organ and Tissue Donation Awareness Week](https://www.blood.ca/en/about-us/media/organ-and-tissue-donation/backgrounder-national-organ-and-tissue-donation-awareness-week) in Canada! Every year, this week is held during the last full week of April to raise awareness about the critical need for more donors across the country and encourage Canadians to register their decision and talk to their loved ones about organ donation. Register now to become an organ and tissue donor at [organtissuedonation.ca](https://organtissuedonation.ca/)!
DOWNS: It's [Grey Cup Sunday](https://www.greycupfestival.ca/) – time for some Canadian football! In the CFL, teams have just three downs to advance the ball ten yards, compared to four in American football. That rule gives the Canadian game its faster pace and wide-open plays. The three-down system has long been a point of pride in Canada, encouraging bold passes, big runs, and thrilling Grey Cup finishes!
DRESS: Red Dress Day, also known as the National Day of Awareness for Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls and Two-Spirit People, is observed annually on May 5th. The day honours and brings awareness to the thousands of Indigenous women, girls and two-spirit people who have been subject to disproportionate violence in Canada. Red Dress Day was inspired by Métis artist Jaime Black’s REDress Project installation, in which she hung empty, red dresses to represent the missing and murdered women. Red dresses have become symbolic of the crisis as a result of her installation.
DRIED: Pemmican is a nutrient-rich food made from dried meat, tallow, and sometimes dried berries. Traditionally prepared by Indigenous Peoples in parts of North America, it has long been valued for its long shelf life and high energy content, making it an essential food for survival, particularly during long journeys across Canada's vast landscapes. Pemmican can be eaten raw or used in prepared meals, and it remains part of Indigenous cuisine today. The word pemmican comes from the Cree word 'pimikan,' meaning 'manufactured grease.'
DRINK: One of Canada’s most iconic drinks, the Caesar, was invented in Calgary in 1969 by bartender Walter Chell to celebrate the opening of an Italian restaurant at the Calgary Inn. Inspired by spaghetti alle vongole, he mixed vodka, Clamato juice, Worcestershire sauce and hot sauce, and the Caesar was born. Canadians are estimated to drink more than 400 million Caesars each year, making it one of the country’s most popular cocktails.
DRIVE: In Canada’s history, the cattle drive was an essential part of the ranching culture, especially in the western provinces. In the late 1800s, cowboys would drive herds of cattle across vast distances to railheads, where the animals were shipped to markets. These cattle drives, especially in areas like Alberta and Saskatchewan, were grueling yet vital to the growth of Canada’s beef industry. The tradition of cattle driving is still celebrated today in rodeos and ranching festivals, reminding Canadians of the tough, adventurous spirit that shaped the nation’s prairies.
DRONE: On a vast swath of southern Alberta prairie, near the tiny village of Foremost, unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) have unrivalled freedom to roam. The Foremost UAS Test Range offers more than 700 square nautical miles of restricted airspace, making it uniquely positioned to advance Canada’s drone technology development. This gives small and medium-sized firms plenty of space to test new drone technologies. It is one of only two places approved by Transport Canada to conduct beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) testing.
DRUID: Modern druidry has taken root in Canada, where groups gather to celebrate the changing seasons, honour nature, and explore Celtic-inspired spiritual traditions. From coastal ceremonies in Atlantic Canada to forest gatherings in British Columbia, Canadian druids blend ancient symbolism with local landscapes, reminding us how deeply connected many Canadians feel to the land around them.
DRYER: The word dryer is forever tied to Sidney Crosby's rise to hockey greatness. Growing up in Cole Harbour, Nova Scotia, Crosby spent hours shooting pucks in the basement of his childhood home, and the family clothes dryer bore the marks of many slapshots sent its way. This makeshift training ground played a part in shaping Crosby into the NHL legend he became. In fact, the battered dryer was even featured in an exhibit at the [Nova Scotia Sport Hall of Fame](https://nsshf.com/), a testament to the role it played in his journey. Now, as he leads Team Canada as captain in the 4 Nations Face-Off, Crosby continues to inspire the next generation of hockey stars.
DULSE: Somewhat of an acquired taste, dulse is an edible red seaweed that grows in intertidal zones in the North Atlantic and Northwest Pacific Oceans. Dulse picked off the coast of Grand Manan Island, New Brunswick in Canada's Bay of Fundy is said to be the best in the world, specifically that harvested in Dark Harbour.
DUNES: The world's smallest desert can be found in the Yukon! In truth, the moniker is used in good fun as the Carcross Desert isn't a desert at all. The beautiful 2.5 square kilometre patch of land is a series of sand dunes left over from a glacial lake thousands of years ago. The tiny area is kept dry year-round thanks to the surrounding mountains. In contrast, the Athabasca Sand Dunes in Saskatchewan is the largest active sand surface in Canada at 1925 km² and one of the world's most northerly major sand dunes.
EARLY: Natural Resources Canada has developed a national [Earthquake Early Warning](https://www.earthquakescanada.nrcan.gc.ca/eew-asp/system-en.php) (EEW) system designed to provide early detection and warning in areas of moderate to high earthquake hazard and with concentrations of population and infrastructure. In Canada, this earthquake risk is concentrated in western British Columbia, eastern Ontario, and southern Quebec. The EEW system began operation in BC in the spring of 2024 and will begin in Quebec and Ontario in early 2025.
EARTH: Happy Earth Day! 🌎 Every year on April 22, [Earth Day](https://earthday.ca/) marks the anniversary of the birth of the modern environmental movement in 1970. In 1990, the creation of the organization in France and in Canada goes hand in hand with the internationalization of the Earth Day movement. Earth Day in 1990 became a global celebration, with participation by an estimated 200 million people in at least 136 countries. Over the years, Earth Day has become the largest participatory environmental movement on the planet.
EATER: The Smoke Eaters (aka Smokies) have existed as both junior and senior hockey teams in Canada since the 1920s. The senior Smoke Eaters won two Allan Cup championships, 1938 and 1962, and two Ice Hockey World Championships playing for Canada in 1939 and 1961. The senior Smokies were the last independent ice hockey club to represent Canada in international competition before the Canada men's national ice hockey team was established in 1963. The current Trail Smoke Eaters are a junior A ice hockey team from Trail, British Columbia, that are part of the British Columbia Hockey League. Learn more about the Smoke Eaters in [Craig Baird's Canadian History Ehx podcast episode](https://canadaehx.com/2022/01/11/the-trail-smoke-eaters-2/)!
EAVES: In Canada, the term "eavestroughs" is commonly used to refer to the rain gutters attached to the eaves of a roof! While "gutters" is the more common term elsewhere, Canadians prefer "eavestroughs" to describe these important drainage systems that help manage rainfall and protect buildings from water damage. This uniquely Canadian term reflects the country's distinctive linguistic features and regional vocabulary!
EIDER: The [common eider](https://www.hww.ca/en/wildlife/birds/common-eider.html) is a large sea duck that inhabits Arctic and Subarctic coastal marine habitats. The common eider has a distinctive long wedge-shaped bill and is the largest duck in the northern hemisphere. Common eiders breed on marine coasts from Alaska and Arctic islands along ponds and lagoons near the ocean from Husdon Bay and James Bay and along the East Coast as far south as Maine. This species has been identified as a priority for conservation and/or stewardship in one or more Bird Conservation Region Strategies in Canada.
EIGHT: Canada has a proud tradition in rowing, especially in the men's and women's eight events. The coxed eight boat class (8 rowers with one oar each and a coxswain to steer) has been Canada's most successful rowing event with notable triumphs on the world stage. The Canadian men's and women's eight teams have collectively won a total of six Olympic medals: two golds and four silvers.
ELDER: Elders are respected individuals who play key roles in Indigenous communities. They are important knowledge keepers, and they also help to ensure cultural continuity.
ELECT: Canada is a representative democracy. During an election, all Canadian citizens who are at least 18 years old on election day can vote in their electoral district.
ELVES: [Santa's Village](https://www.santasvillage.ca/) in Bracebridge, Ontario, isn't just a magical summer home for Santa - it's also home to his hardworking 'elves'! Nestled at the 45th parallel, halfway between the North Pole and the equator, it's the perfect spot for Santa’s summer retreat. Since opening in 1955, this charming theme park has welcomed families from near and far, offering a whimsical experience full of holiday cheer during its seasonal operation. The employees - playfully known as elves - help create a world of enchantment, making Santa's Village one of Ontario's most beloved family destinations.
EMBER: [Girl Guides of Canada](https://www.girlguides.ca/) (GGC) announced a new branch name for girls ages 7 and 8 in 2023, replacing the name Brownies with Embers. GGC implemented the name change after hearing from current and former members that the previous name caused harm and was a barrier to belonging for racialized girls and women. With the new Embers name, the hope is that even more girls will see Guiding as a space where they can just be themselves.
EPOXY: Hockey sticks have come a long way from their wooden roots. Many high-performance sticks today are made from layers of carbon fibre bonded with epoxy resin, creating a strong, lightweight composite that can flex and spring back during a shot. Epoxy helps hold those layers together while withstanding the repeated stress and impacts of Canada’s national winter sport.
ERUPT: Many Canadians are unaware that western Canada lies along the Pacific "Ring of Fire" and has active volcanoes. In fact, there have been at least 49 volcanic eruptions in British Columbia and the Yukon Territory during the last 10,000 years. The most recent eruption in Canada took place at Lava Fork in northwestern B.C. about 150 years ago. Learn more about Canada's volcanoes on NRCan's [Volcanoes Canada](https://chis.nrcan.gc.ca/volcano-volcan/can-vol-en.php) website.
FACES: [Faces Magazine](https://facesmag.ca/) is Ottawa’s premier lifestyle publication, showcasing the faces behind the city's businesses, sports, and entertainment scene. Faces highlights the best of Ottawa with a uniquely Canadian flair. From restaurants to community leaders, it’s all about connecting people and celebrating what makes the capital great!
FAIRS: With the arrival of the autumn season, Canadians have been attending fairs that celebrate the agricultural heritage and community spirit across the country. These fairs showcase everything from livestock competitions and crafts to local produce, giving visitors a chance to experience the rich bounty of the harvest season. Many fairs feature rides, games and entertainment, along with traditional activities such as pie-eating contests, barn dances, and exhibitions that highlight the skills of local artisans and farmers. These cherished events not only connect communities but also remind us of the importance of agriculture in Canada’s history and culture.
FAIRY: At Fairy Lake in British Columbia, a tiny tree stands as a symbol of resilience! Perched on a submerged log, this Douglas Fir, often called the "Bonsai Tree," has defied the odds by growing in the middle of the lake. With no soil and limited nutrients, it thrives solely from the decaying log beneath it. This magical sight has made Fairy Lake a favourite spot for photographers and nature lovers alike - proof that even the smallest trees can stand tall!
FALSE: Pacific Central Station is a railway station in Vancouver, British Columbia, which acts as the western terminus of Via Rail's cross-country service. The station is located in the False Creek area of Vancouver and is a handsome illustration of Beaux-Arts architectural principles, retaining both the exterior features and interior detailing typical of the style. Designed by the Canadian Northern Railway to serve as the western terminus of its transcontinental route, it was originally named False Creek Station and was designated a heritage railway station in 1991.
FEAST: Réveillon is a traditional all-night feast that starts after church service on Christmas Eve and lasts until the wee hours of Christmas morning. First celebrated in 19th-century France, the Canadian menu includes tourtière (a meat pie made with pork and beef or veal), ragoût de pattes de cochon (pigs' feet stew) and bûche de Nöel (a Yule log dessert). This celebration and the traditions and foods associated with it speak to the history of francophones across Canada.
FETES: Joyeuse Fête nationale! The word fête is borrowed from French, where it means “festival” or “party” – and it’s also recognized in English to describe a lively celebration. In Québec, fêtes reach their peak on June 24 for La Fête nationale du Québec, also known as [Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/celebrate-canada/saint-jean-baptiste-day.html). It’s a province-wide party filled with music, fireworks, parades, and pride in French Canadian culture – a true fête in every sense of the word!
FIELD: There are so many different types of fields in Canada: sports fields, wheat fields, oil fields, and ice fields to name a few. The Canadian Prairies are known for their open skies and vast fields of grain, but Canada is also home to the world's largest non-polar ice field in the St. Elias Mountains located in Kluane National Park and Reserve, Yukon Territory.
FIRES: Fires have been a natural part of Canada’s landscapes for thousands of years, shaping forests, grasslands, and wildlife habitats. Indigenous peoples have long used controlled burns to renew the land and support healthy ecosystems. Today, wildfire season, which peaks from spring through late summer, remains an important part of life in Canada. Modern wildfire management combines skilled crews, advanced technology, and careful planning to protect communities and the environment while respecting fire’s natural role in the ecosystem.
FLIRT: [Flirt Drinks](https://flirtdrinks.com/) is a Canadian company founded in Quebec's Outaouais region by two lifelong friends determined to reduce food waste. Their Flirt sparkling lemonades are made with rescued fruit that might otherwise be discarded, turning a simple idea into a refreshing made-in-Canada success story. Cheers to a Canadian company finding a fresh way to make every piece of fruit count!
FLOOD: [Flooding](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/floods-and-flood-control) stands as Canada's most frequent and expensive natural disaster. In fact, floods account for 40% of weather-related disasters in the country! From spring ice jams in the Red River Valley to coastal storm surges in the Maritimes, flooding can impact communities across the country. Some of Canada's most significant floods include the 2013 Alberta floods, which caused billions in damages, and the 1997 "Flood of the Century" in Manitoba. With climate change increasing extreme weather events, Canada continues to invest in flood prevention to keep communities safe from rising waters.
FLORA: Happy First Day of Spring! Canada is home to an incredibly diverse range of flora, with over 19,000 plant species thriving across its vast and varied landscapes. From the rugged peaks of the Rockies to the lush coastal rainforests of the Pacific Northwest, Canada's plant life reflects its diverse climate and geography. Among its most iconic species is the maple tree, a symbol of Canadian identity proudly displayed on the national flag. As spring arrives, Canada's flora comes to life, painting the landscape with vibrant colours and fresh growth!
FLOUR: What makes iconic Canadian glacial lakes like Moraine Lake and Lake Louise so blue? Rock flour or glacier flour of course! The small particles of rock flour find their way to the lake via melting streams. Glacial flour being so light, is suspended in the water. This murky appearance is referred to as glacial milk. The more of this glacial milk mixture there is, the more turquoise the glacial lake appears!
FLUTE: To generations of Canadians, the opening flute of [Hinterland Who's Who](https://www.hww.ca/) is instantly recognizable. The vignettes also had an immense impact on Canadian culture. The series was produced for the Canadian Wildlife Service by the National Film Board to generate interest in Canada's wildlife through one-minute long segments that could air during commercial breaks.. The first Hinterland Who's Who debuted in 1963 and featured John Cacavas' Flute Poem to open the vignette. Then, the voice of naturalist John Livingston came on to describe the animal in the footage.
FLYER: When it made its debut at the 1953 [Canadian National Exhibition](https://www.theex.com/) in Toronto, The Flyer roller coaster was the highest and fastest in the world at the time. Its tallest point was 19 m or 62 ft, and it could reach speeds up to 104 km or 65 miles per hour. Two four-car trains sped along the ride's 796 m or 2,612 ft long track for a total of 32 riders per train.
FORKS: The Forks, located in Winnipeg at the junction of the Red and Assiniboine rivers, has been a meeting place for over 6,000 years. Indigenous peoples traded at The Forks, followed by European fur traders, Scottish settlers, railway pioneers and tens of thousands of immigrants. The Forks was designated a National Historic Site of Canada in 1974 due to its status as a cultural landscape. The Canadian Museum for Human Rights is located on Indigenous ancestral lands just adjacent to The Forks.
FREED: On April 17, Canada marks the anniversary of the [Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms](https://www.justice.gc.ca/eng/csj-sjc/rfc-dlc/ccrf-ccdl/), a key part of our Constitution that protects the freedoms and rights of all Canadians. The Charter guarantees basic rights, such as freedom of thought, expression, and peaceful assembly, while ensuring equality for all citizens. It's a reminder that freedoms like these are fundamental to our democracy and way of life.
FRIES: Canadians consumed over 240,000 metric tonnes of frozen fries in 2019.
FROND: Along British Columbia’s Pacific coastline, towering forests of bull kelp create underwater canopies of long, leafy fronds that provide shelter for marine life and help protect coastal ecosystems. Growing up to 30 centimetres a day, a single bull kelp frond can become part of a vast underwater forest that helps buffer shorelines against powerful Pacific storm waves. A remarkable example of how Canada’s ocean forests help shape and protect the coast.
FROST: Canadian winters can be freezing cold. Uncovered skin in freezing temperatures can get frostbite. But that doesn't stop Canadians from having outdoor winter festivals! [Frost Regina](https://frostregina.com/) was just held in Regina, Saskatchewan from Feb 3-12, 2023. This unique city-wide event celebrates the cold winter climate through stunning light installations, local music, captivating art, and rich culture. Frost Regina is where winter comes to life!
FUNDY: The Bay of Fundy, located between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, is home to the highest tides in the world – reaching up to 16 metres! This natural wonder fills and empties twice daily, moving over 160 billion tonnes of seawater. It’s also a hotspot for fossil discoveries, coastal hikes, and whale watching. Whether you're exploring Hopewell Rocks or catching a tidal bore, the Bay of Fundy is pure Canadian magic!
GAMES: The Canada Games is a multi-sport event held every two years, alternating between the Canada Winter Games and the Canada Summer Games. They represent the highest level of national competition for Canadian athletes. The [Niagara 2022 Canada Summer Games](https://www.canadagames.ca/previous-games/niagara-2022) will take place Aug 6-21, 2022!
GASES: Happy [Earth Day](https://earthday.ca/)! Did you know that Canada's veteran satellite, [SCISAT](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/satellites/scisat/), has been orbiting Earth 15 times a day for over 21 years? It's the only satellite in the world that can monitor all the regulated gases covered by the Montreal Protocol – an international agreement to protect the ozone layer. SCISAT helps scientists around the globe track the impact of over 70 gases in our atmosphere, playing a vital role in efforts to reduce harmful emissions and combat climate change.
GATES: The Queen's Gates is the formal entrance to Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Ontario. The Princes' Gates is a triumphal arch and a monumental gateway at Exhibition Place in Toronto, Ontario. Canada Gate was installed in London, England in the early years of the 20th century as part of the memorial to Queen Victoria. The gates were a gift from Canada, celebrating its contribution to the then British Empire.
GAVEL: Did you know that despite what movies and television shows might suggest, the iconic courtroom gavel is largely absent from Canada's justice system and Parliament? Following British tradition, Canadian judges, including those of the Supreme Court of Canada, do not use gavels, and neither does the Speaker of the House of Commons. Instead, order is maintained through voice, procedure, and long-standing tradition rather than a symbolic tap of wood found in many legislatures elsewhere.
GENRE: The [Juno Awards](https://junoawards.ca/) celebrate the diversity of Canadian music across multiple genres, from pop and rock to country, hip-hop, jazz, and beyond! Since their inception in 1970, the Junos have evolved to reflect Canada's rich musical landscape, adding new genre categories over the years to spotlight emerging talent. Whether it's indie, electronic, or traditional Indigenous music, the Junos showcase the best of Canada's sound! Tonight, the Junos return to Vancouver, British Columbia, marking the city's fifth time hosting Canada's biggest night in music!
GHOST: BOO! Ghost stories are always much creepier when they hit close to home! From gothic hotels to gruesome battlefields, Canada is home to numerous spooky sites from coast to coast! Some of the most haunted places in Canada include: the Fairmont Banff Springs Hotel, the Hockey Hall of Fame and Keg Mansion in Toronto, the Fairmont Château Laurier and Jail Hostel in Ottawa, the Tranquille Sanatorium in Kamloops, the Fairmont Empress Hotel in Victoria, and the Plains of Abraham in Quebec City. Are you brave enough to visit them?
GIANT: The Sibley Peninsula just outside of Thunder Bay, Ontario is home to The Sleeping Giant, a series of cliffs which resemble a giant lying on its back. The formation is part of Sleeping Giant Provincial Park and it was voted number one on a list of The Seven Wonders of Canada, and 2007 competition sponsored by CBC. Another famous Canadian giant was "The Friendly Giant", a children's television program that aired on CBC from 1958-1985 with over 3,000 episodes!
GILET: A gilet is a sleeveless vest designed to provide warmth while keeping arms free for movement. In Canada, this practical layer is a favourite among hikers, cyclists, paddlers, and outdoor enthusiasts who need extra insulation during cool mornings and evenings. Whether exploring a national park or opening the cottage for the season, a gilet is a versatile piece of clothing built for Canada’s changing weather.
GLASS: [The Bottle Houses](https://bottlehouses.com/) in Cape Egmont, Prince Edward Island was built in 1980 by Édouard Arsenault. It is a must-see tourist attraction that includes life-sized buildings made of over 25,000 recycled coloured glass bottles. The village contains a six-gabled house, a tavern, and a chapel in a tranquil garden setting. The Bottle Houses opens for the 2024 season on May 18th so add it to your summer travel list!
GOLDEN: Canada’s newest team in the Professional Women’s Hockey League is ready to shine on the West Coast – introducing the [Vancouver Goldeneyes](https://www.thepwhl.com/en/teams/vancouver-goldeneyes)! Their name is inspired by the goldeneye duck, a hardy Pacific Northwest native known for its speed and sharp vision. The Goldeneyes bring a new burst of energy to Canada’s women’s hockey scene, and Vancouver fans can’t wait to cheer on their “golden” crew as they take flight in the PWHL.
GONCH: Happy National Underwear Day! In Canadian slang, gonch is one of several playful words for underwear – right up there with gitch, gotch, and gonchies! Most popular in Western Canada, gonch has become part of our quirky national vocab. Whether you’re folding your gitch or packing spare gonch for a weekend at the cabin, it’s a uniquely Canadian way to talk about your unmentionables!
GOOSE: A subspecies known as “giant” Canada geese are the largest geese in the world.
GORGE: Canada is home to some incredible gorges & canyons. One of the best-known canyons in Ontario is the Niagara Gorge, which starts at the base of Niagara Falls, and it ends 11 km downriver, near the town of Queenston, where the famous falls originated some 14,000 years ago. Other notable gorges/canyons in Canada include: Elora Gorge (Ontario's Grand Canyon!), Eau Claire Gorge (Ontario), Grand Falls Gorge (New Brunswick), Coaticook Gorge (Quebec), Ouimet Canyon (Thunder Bay, Ontario), Maligne Canyon (Alberta), Nahanni Canyons (Northwest Territories), Canyon Sainte-Anne (Quebec City, Quebec), and Horseshoe Canyon (Alberta).
GORSE: Gorse is an invasive shrub found in Canada, primarily in British Columbia. This evergreen, spiny plant has bright yellow, pea-like flowers and often grows in disturbed areas like roadsides, pastures, and burned lands. Originally brought from Europe for hedges and livestock shelter, gorse can spread quickly, crowding out native plants. Despite its challenges, those golden blooms provide early-season nectar for pollinators, brightening the Canadian landscape.
GOURD: Happy Thanksgiving! With their bright colours and unusual shapes, a variety of gourds are sure to be decorating Canadian dinner tables this weekend. Although pumpkins, squash and gourds are all part of the Cucurbitaceae family, gourds are not edible and are grown for their ornamental value. On the other hand, very edible pumpkin pie will be the dessert of choice in Canada for Thanksgiving!
GRADE: September in Canada means back to school! Students head into a new grade, ready for fresh notebooks, sharpened pencils, and new adventures in learning. Grades mark more than just progress – they’re milestones filled with growth, challenges, and proud moments. In Quebec, high school finishes at Grade 11, after which students move on to CEGEP to continue their studies. No matter where they are in the country, every grade is a step forward in the journey of learning.
GRAIN: The grain sector is a key driver of Canada's economic growth, exporting 26.4 million tonnes of wheat in 2020-21 and over $25 billion in exports sales.
GRAPE: In Canada, the two main commercial grape-growing areas are southern Ontario's Niagara Peninsula and the Okanagan and neighbouring Similkameen Valleys in south-central British Columbia. In 2022, approximately 33,000 acres were used for the cultivation of grapes in Canada. The main grape vine varieties grown in Canada are Chardonnay, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Riesling. Wineries take about 80% of the annual grape production in Canada.
GRASS: In Indigenous culture, braided sweet grass is believed to attract good spirits, energies, and influences. Sweet grass, with its sweet aroma reminding people of the love, kindness, and gentleness provided by Mother Earth, is known to have a calming effect and is often used during talking circles and healings. Sweet grass is often used during smudging to call in the good Spirit.
GRAVE: Happy Halloween from Canuckle! 🎃 Halloween is the perfect time to explore some of Canada's most haunted grave sites. One eerie spot is Fairview Lawn Cemetery in Halifax, where victims of the Titanic disaster were laid to rest. Many visitors report strange occurrences near the graves, with whispers of spirits lingering on the grounds. Another spooky destination is Victoria’s Ross Bay Cemetery in British Columbia, where tales of ghostly apparitions wandering among the graves keep visitors on edge. Canada's haunted history runs deep, and during the Halloween season, these grave sites become even more chilling!
GREBE: The grebe is a type of water bird commonly found in Canada, especially in wetlands and lakes. Known for their striking appearance and elaborate mating dances, grebes are expert swimmers and divers. Some species, like the Western Grebe, even perform synchronized "rushing" displays, where they dash across the water's surface together in a spectacular show of coordination!
GROWN: From PEI potatoes to Alberta beef, and Saskatchewan wheat to Québec maple syrup, so many delicious things are proudly grown right here in Canada! Our vast and diverse landscape supports everything from fresh berries to sweet corn, producing some of the finest ingredients and products the world has to offer.
GUIDE: Girl Guides of Canada started on September 7, 1910, and Canada was among the founding members of the World Association of Girl Guides and Girl Scouts (WAGGGS) in 1928. Some well-known former Girl Guides include: Queen Elizabeth II, Margaret Atwood, Celine Dion, Sarah McLachlan, and Dr. Roberta Bondar, who juggled Girl Guide cookies in space!
HEADS: The heads side of a Canadian coin features a portrait of the reigning monarch. For over 70 years, it was Queen Elizabeth II - making hers the longest reign ever depicted on Canadian currency. In 2023, Canada introduced new coins with King Charles III on the heads side, facing left, continuing the royal tradition of alternating profile directions with each new monarch!
HEATS: In Olympic racing events, heats are the preliminary rounds that decide who advances to the finals. From short-track speed skating to snowboarding and skiing, Canadian athletes push hard in every heat, giving fans a front-row view of the skill, speed, and determination that define Team Canada at the Games.
HEIST: Over the course of several months in 2011 and 2012, a team of thieves stole approximately 2,700 tonnes of maple syrup from a strategic maple syrup reserve maintained in Quebec. The theft has been popularly dubbed as the [Great Canadian Maple Syrup Heist](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/great-canadian-maple-syrup-heist). At the time of the heist, the stolen maple syrup was valued at nearly $18 million. The heist may be one of the largest thefts in Canadian history.
HIDES: On May 15, we mark [Moose Hide Campaign Day](https://moosehidecampaign.ca/), a national day of action for the Indigenous-led grassroots movement to engage men and boys in ending violence towards women and children. The Moose Hide Campaign began with a small patch of moose hide, worn as a symbol of commitment to safety and healing. Today, millions across Canada wear these hides to stand up against gender-based violence. To support them in igniting powerful change, please consider [donating to the Moose Hide Campaign](https://moosehidecampaign.ca/donate/) today.
HIKES: National Parks Day is the perfect time to lace up your boots and explore some of Canada’s incredible hikes. Trek the rugged peaks of Banff and Jasper in Alberta, discover the fjords and unique geology of Gros Morne in Newfoundland, wander ancient forests in Fundy National Park, or take in coastal views at Pacific Rim National Park Reserve in British Columbia. Each park offers unforgettable adventures and stunning landscapes – grab your boots and hit the trail!
HOCUS: From 1981 to 1987, the Canadian children’s show Today’s Special brought magic to the screen for over 120 episodes. Set in a Toronto department store, the magic words “Hocus Pocus Alimagocus!” would bring Jeff the mannequin to life! The adventures of Jeff, Jodie, Sam Crenshaw, and Muffy Mouse delighted generations of viewers and made everyday moments feel truly magical.
HOWLS: Wolves are known for their haunting howls, a form of communication used to signal territory, locate pack members, or coordinate hunting. In Canada, grey wolves roam vast regions from the forests of British Columbia to the tundra of Nunavut, and their howls echo across the wilderness, a timeless sound of the country’s wild landscapes.
HYDRA: Hydra was a crucial and secure radio communications link in Canada during the Second World War. Part of [Camp X](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/camp-x) (a training school for covert agents and a radio communications centre that operated on the shores of Lake Ontario between Whitby and Oshawa), Hydra sent and received Allied radio (including telegraph) signals from around the world. Hydra was the most sophisticated telecommunications centre of its time and was instrumental in coding/decoding information vital to the allied war effort.
JETON: Jetons are small tokens once used for counting and calculations long before modern calculators existed. Today, examples of jetons are part of the national currency collection at the [Bank of Canada Museum](https://www.bankofcanadamuseum.ca/collection/name/view/10/32/74/jeton), highlighting early tools connected to money and commerce. They remind us that even simple objects played an important role in the history of finance in Canada and beyond.
KARAT: Gold is Canada's most valuable mined commodity, with a production value of $13.7 billion in 2021. Gold is mined in 10 Canadian provinces and territories, with the majority coming from Ontario and Quebec that together accounted for 70% of mined gold production in Canada in 2021. Canadian mines produced 223 tonnes of gold in 2021, ranking Canada as the fourth-largest global producer.
KARST: [Karst landforms](https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/karst-landform) are shaped by water dissolving soluble rock, creating caves, sinkholes and underground waterways. Vancouver Island is home to extensive karst landscapes and one of Canada’s greatest concentrations of caves. Its ARGO cave system stretches 25.45 kilometres through 250-million-year-old limestone, making it Canada’s longest known cave.
KINGS: Today is [Commonwealth Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/important-commemorative-days/commonwealth-day.html)! The 56 member countries of the Commonwealth, including Canada, celebrate Commonwealth Day every year on the second Monday in March. It is a day of observance by more than 2 billion citizens of their common bonds and the contribution of the Commonwealth to the creation of a harmonious global environment. Canada has been a monarchy for centuries - first under the kings of France in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, then under the British Crown in the 18th and 19th centuries, and now as a kingdom in her own right.
LABEL: More than ever, Canadians are looking to the label to guide their choices. Amid rising trade tensions and growing national pride, more shoppers are seeking out goods labelled “Made in Canada” and “Product of Canada.” A recent survey found that 84% of Canadians check labels to see where items are made, and 77% say they’ll choose Canadian – even if it costs more. That little label is a symbol of pride, connecting Canadians to the people and places behind every product.
LAGER: The top selling style of beer in Canada is, by far, the pale lager. December 10th is National Lager Day in Canada!
LAKER: Lakers are massive freighters built to carry bulk Canadian cargo, including grain, iron ore, salt, and limestone. Since the late 19th century, they have hauled raw materials from docks in the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence Seaway to the industrial centres of Ontario and Quebec. Many lakers are specially designed with narrow beams and long hulls to fit the waterways’ locks and channels, making them unique to Canada’s inland shipping routes.
LAKES: Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world combined! Almost 9% of Canada's total surface area is covered by freshwater.
LARCH: Larches are among the dominant plants in the boreal forests of Canada. Larches are the only Canadian deciduous conifers, turning golden and shedding all their leaves in fall.
LASER: Canadians Bruce Kirby and Ian Bruce invented the iconic Laser sailboat. The Laser became one of the world's most popular racing sailboats. It became so popular that the Olympic committee added the Laser as an Olympic-class boat for men in 1996 and women in 2008. The Laser’s enduring popularity, though, comes from the thousands of recreational sailors who experience the pure pleasure of single-handing a Laser on a breezy day.
LATTE: September 29th was National Coffee Day! Did you know that lattes are one of the most popular coffee beverages in Canada? In fact, Canadians drink over 1.5 billion cups of coffee annually, with lattes being a go-to choice at many coffee shops. Approximately 7 in 10 Canadians drink coffee daily, making it the most popular beverage in Canada. Whether you prefer it hot or iced, the latte has firmly secured its place in Canada's coffee culture, keeping Canadians caffeinated coast to coast!
LAYER: Nanaimo Bars are a Canadian dessert staple originating in Nanaimo, a city on Vancouver Island in British Columbia. It consists of three layers: a graham wafer crumb and shredded coconut base, a custard-flavoured butter icing filling, and a chocolate ganache topping. The Nanaimo bar was popularized nationwide after being highlighted as a classic Canadian dessert at Expo 86. In 2006, the Nanaimo bar was declared Canada’s favourite confection by a reader’s poll in the National Post.
LICKS: Lick's was a homegrown Canadian burger restaurant that first opened on Queen Street East in Toronto in 1980 and grew to more than 30 locations across Ontario.
